title: The trim family
description:
Lesson 1.02 shows a reference page for `trim_left`. Implement it, and its "see also" functions `trim_right` and `trim`, exactly as documented:

```cpp-norun
std::string trim_left(std::string_view s, std::string_view chars = " \t\n");    // (1)
std::string trim_left(std::string_view s, char c);                               // (2)
std::string trim_right(std::string_view s, std::string_view chars = " \t\n");   // (3)
std::string trim_right(std::string_view s, char c);                              // (4)
std::string trim(std::string_view s, std::string_view chars = " \t\n");         // (5)
std::string trim(std::string_view s, char c);                                    // (6)
```

1. Removes every leading character that appears in `chars`. If `chars` is empty, nothing is removed.
2. Removes every leading character equal to `c`.
3. and 4. are the same at the **end** of `s`.
5. and 6. remove from **both** ends.

**Return value**: a copy of `s` without the removed characters; an empty string if every character is removed. Characters are compared as single bytes.
hints: `std::string_view::find(char)` returns `npos` when the character is not in the set, which makes "is this character one of `chars`?" a single call. An empty set then removes nothing by itself.
The `char` overloads can call the `string_view` ones with a one-character view: `std::string_view(&c, 1)`.
